contribution: The energy bookkeeping of the first law extends to powers: heat transfers by conduction, convection and thermal radiation, the power conducted through a building part is $P = UA\Delta T$, and the temperature of an object stays constant when the power coming into it and the power leaving it are equal, which explains the greenhouse effect and climate change.
learn: You recognise the ways heat transfers: conduction, convection and thermal radiation.
You can calculate the thermal power conducted through a building part.
You can use energy balance to explain the greenhouse effect and climate change.
prior: Heat and work change internal energy, $\Delta U = Q + W$, and energy is conserved (chapter *Internal energy, heat and conservation of energy*)
Heat is the transfer of energy from hotter to colder because of a temperature difference (chapter *Internal energy, heat and conservation of energy*)

activities.text: The Moon is on average as far from the Sun as the Earth, and the same amount of sunlight hits each square metre of its surface. However, the Moon has no atmosphere, and the mean temperature of its surface is well below freezing. The same difference can be seen on a small scale on Earth: on a clear winter night the frost gets harsher quickly, but on a cloudy night the temperature falls only a little.
activities.question: The atmosphere does not produce energy itself. How can it still keep the ground warmer than it would be without it?

activities.title: Review from the previous lesson
activities.prompt: In chapter *Internal energy, heat and conservation of energy*, the change in internal energy was written as $\Delta U = Q + W$. Every minute, 600 J of heat transfers from the stove to the water in a pan, and every minute 600 J of heat transfers from the water to the surroundings. No work is done. What happens to the internal energy and the temperature of the water?

choices.text: The internal energy increases, because heat keeps coming into the water.
choices.feedback: Only the net transfer changes the internal energy. 600 J comes into the water and 600 J leaves it every minute, so $Q = 600\,\text{J} - 600\,\text{J} = 0$ and $\Delta U = 0$.

choices.text: The internal energy and the temperature stay constant.
choices.feedback: Correct. In a minute $Q = +600\,\text{J} - 600\,\text{J} = 0$ and $W = 0$, so $\Delta U = Q + W = 0$. When the energy coming in and the energy going out are equal, the temperature does not change.

choices.text: The internal energy decreases, because heat keeps leaving the water.
choices.feedback: The heat leaving would decrease the internal energy only if it were not replaced. Here as much comes into the water as leaves it, so $\Delta U = 0$.

choices.text: You cannot tell without the temperature of the water.
choices.feedback: The first law is enough: $\Delta U = Q + W$, and here $Q = 0$ and $W = 0$ every minute. You do not need the temperature to decide whether the internal energy changes.

activities.title: Prediction 1: why is the ground warmer?
activities.prompt: Without an atmosphere the mean temperature of the ground would be about −18 °C, but it is about +15 °C. Three students explain the difference. Whose explanation do you think is the best?

choices.text: Aino: The atmosphere is like a blanket that stops heat from being conducted from the ground into space.
choices.feedback: How can energy transfer from the ground into empty space, where there are no particles? Look at the table in the Investigate stage to see what power comes to the ground and what it radiates with and without the atmosphere.

choices.text: Bea: The gases of the atmosphere radiate part of the thermal radiation of the ground back down, so the ground receives energy in addition to the Sun.
choices.feedback: The table in the Investigate stage tests this: compare how much power comes to the ground and how much it radiates with and without the atmosphere.

choices.text: Cem: The atmosphere stores the energy of the Sun and more and more of it accumulates all the time, so the ground is warm.
choices.feedback: If energy kept accumulating, the Earth would keep warming and its temperature would not stay at about +15 °C. At a steady temperature the power coming in and the power going out must be equal. In the table of the Investigate stage you can check whether these balances hold.

activities.title: Prediction 2: when carbon dioxide is added
activities.prompt: The carbon dioxide concentration of the atmosphere is raised to a higher value all at once and then kept constant. The power coming from the Sun does not change. What happens to the temperature of the Earth after that?

choices.text: Aino: The Earth warms only as long as the concentration increases. When the concentration stays constant, the warming stops immediately.
choices.feedback: The temperature changes as long as the power coming in and the power going out differ, not as long as the concentration changes. In the second table of the Investigate stage the concentration is constant from the row "just after" onwards: check whether the extra power is then zero straight away.

choices.text: Bea: At first less power leaves into space than comes in. The Earth warms until the power leaving is again equal.
choices.feedback: The second table of the Investigate stage tests this: follow how the power leaving into space and the extra power change as the Earth warms.

choices.text: Cem: The Earth warms without limit, because the extra carbon dioxide keeps trapping more and more energy.
choices.feedback: A warmer object radiates more, so as the Earth warms it radiates more and more into space. In the second table of the Investigate stage you can see what happens to the extra power as the warming proceeds.

activities.title: Predict the radiation of the atmosphere downwards
activities.prompt: Next you study a model of the energy balance of the ground, in which 240 W/m² is absorbed by the ground from the Sun and the ground gives out energy only as thermal radiation. Without an atmosphere the surface radiates 240 W/m² and is in balance (−18 °C). With an atmosphere the surface is in balance at +15 °C and radiates 390 W/m². How much power per square metre must the atmosphere radiate down to the ground?
hints: When the ground is in balance, the power coming into it is equal to the power leaving it.
The ground receives 240 W/m² from the Sun and an unknown power from the atmosphere; the power leaving is 390 W/m².

mistakes.feedback: 390 W/m² is the power radiated by the ground. Part of it is already covered by the 240 W/m² coming from the Sun, and the rest comes from the atmosphere.
You added the powers. In balance the power coming in is equal to the power leaving, 390 W/m², so the share of the atmosphere is the power leaving minus the power coming from the Sun.

activities.solution:
**Given:** with the ground in balance, $P_\text{sun} = 240\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ is absorbed from the Sun and the surface radiates $P_\text{rad} = 390\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$; the surface gives out energy only as thermal radiation

**Find:** the power radiated down by the atmosphere $P_\text{down}$ in $\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$

**Principle:** The temperature of the surface stays constant (+15 °C), so energy neither accumulates in the surface nor decreases: the power coming into the surface is equal to the power leaving it. There are two inputs, the Sun and the thermal radiation radiated down by the atmosphere, and only one output, the radiation of the surface itself.

**Formula:** In balance the power coming in is equal to the power leaving:

$$P_\text{sun} + P_\text{down} = P_\text{rad}$$

$$P_\text{down} = P_\text{rad} - P_\text{sun}$$

**Conversions:** No conversions are needed, because all the powers are given in the same unit $\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$.

**Substitution:** $P_\text{down} = 390\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2} - 240\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2} = 150\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$

**Answer:** $150\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$, three significant figures. The example values $390$ and $240\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ are given as whole numbers, so the difference has the same precision in W/m²; no data limits it any further.

**Reasonableness:** Check the balance: $240 + 150 = 390\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ comes in and $390\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ goes out. The result is positive and smaller than the radiation of the surface, because part of the power leaving is already covered by the Sun. Without an atmosphere $P_\text{down} = 0$ and the surface would radiate only $240\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$, which corresponds to the colder situation.

activities.title: Energy balance of the ground without and with an atmosphere
activities.text:
The table shows the energy balance of the ground as a mean over the whole Earth per square metre. The numbers are calculated with a simple model and are *example values*, not measurements. In the model the power absorbed from the Sun is absorbed entirely by the ground, and the ground gives out energy only as thermal radiation. In reality part of the sunlight is absorbed by the atmosphere, and the ground also gives out energy by convection and by the evaporation of water. In both cases a total of 240 W/m² leaves into space, as much as is absorbed from the Sun.

The column *without* is an Earth with no atmosphere, and the column *with* is an Earth with one. The powers are in W/m².

| Ground | without | with |
|---|---|---|
| absorbed from the Sun | 240 | 240 |
| comes down from the atmosphere | 0 | 150 |
| surface radiates | 240 | 390 |
| temperature | −18 °C | +15 °C |

question.prompt: According to the table, what makes the ground warmer with an atmosphere?

choices.text: More power is absorbed from the Sun when the atmosphere exists.
choices.feedback: The power absorbed from the Sun is the same 240 W/m² in both columns. The difference comes from the second row of the table: look at where else the ground gets energy.

choices.text: 150 W/m² comes down to the ground from the atmosphere, so the surface receives 390 W/m² in total, and in balance it must radiate the same 390 W/m², which requires a higher temperature.
choices.feedback: Correct. The ground receives $240\,\text{W/m}^2 + 150\,\text{W/m}^2 = 390\,\text{W/m}^2$, and in balance the power leaving is equal. The hotter an object is, the more it radiates, so 390 W/m² corresponds to a higher temperature than 240 W/m². The atmosphere does not produce energy: it radiates down part of the radiation it has absorbed from the ground.

choices.text: With an atmosphere the ground radiates less, so more energy is left in the surface.
choices.feedback: In the table the ground radiates more with an atmosphere, 390 W/m² and not 240 W/m². A warmer surface radiates more. The surface still stays in balance, because it also receives more.

choices.text: The atmosphere stops heat from being conducted from the ground into space.
choices.feedback: Energy leaves into space only as radiation, because in a vacuum there are no particles through which heat could be conducted. In the model of the table the ground gives out energy only by radiating, and the difference shows in how much radiation comes to the surface.

activities.title: When the balance is broken
activities.text:
The carbon dioxide concentration of the atmosphere is raised all at once and then kept constant. There are more greenhouse gases, so they absorb more thermal radiation, and at first less power leaves into space than the Earth absorbs. The extra power warms the oceans, the land and the air. In the model the power leaving into space increases by 1.2 W/m² for every kelvin the Earth warms. The table shows the power leaving into space, the excess, that is, the difference between the absorbed power and the power leaving, and the warming $\Delta T$ from the initial situation; the powers are in W/m². The Earth absorbs 240.0 W/m² all the time. The numbers are *example values*; in reality the warming takes decades, because the large heat capacity of the oceans slows it down.

| Stage | Leaves | Excess | $\Delta T$ (K) |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 240.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| just after | 236.4 | 3.6 | 0.0 |
| later | 237.6 | 2.4 | 1.0 |
| later still | 238.8 | 1.2 | 2.0 |

question.prompt: The concentration stays constant from the row "just after" onwards. How many kelvins has the Earth warmed in total when the power leaving is again equal to the power absorbed?
hints: By how much must the power leaving still increase from the value in the row "just after" for the excess to be zero?
The power leaving increases by 1.2 W/m² for every kelvin of warming. Just after the change the excess is 3.6 W/m².

mistakes.feedback: 3.6 is the extra power per square metre (W/m²), not the warming. The power leaving increases by 1.2 W/m² per kelvin, so divide the excess by this.
You multiplied the excess and 1.2 W/m² per kelvin. The question asks how many kelvins are needed for the 3.6 W/m² excess to drop to zero: divide the excess by 1.2 W/m² per kelvin.

question.solution:
**Given:** row "just after" of the table: power leaving $236.4\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ and excess $3.6\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$; absorbed power $240.0\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$; in the model the power leaving increases by $k = 1.2\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2\cdot\text{K}}$ for every kelvin of warming

**Find:** the total warming $\Delta T$ in kelvins when the power leaving is again equal to the power absorbed

**Principle:** The concentration stays constant, so the absorbed power stays the same $240.0\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$. The Earth warms while the excess is positive, and as it warms it radiates more. Balance is reached when the warming has increased the power leaving by exactly the excess.

**Formula:** The power leaving must increase by the excess $\Delta P$, and the increase is $k\,\Delta T$:

$$k\,\Delta T = \Delta P \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Delta T = \frac{\Delta P}{k}$$

**Conversions:** No conversions are needed, because the excess and the coefficient are given in the units $\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ and $\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2\cdot\text{K}}$ and the square metres cancel.

**Substitution:** $\Delta T = \dfrac{3.6\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}}{1.2\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2\cdot\text{K}}} = 3.0\,\text{K}$

**Answer:** $3.0\,\text{K}$, two significant figures. The limiting data are the excess $240.0 - 236.4 = 3.6\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ (the difference has one decimal and two figures) and the coefficient $1.2\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2\cdot\text{K}}$ (two figures).

**Reasonableness:** Check the balance: the power leaving is $236.4 + 1.2 \cdot 3.0 = 240.0\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$, equal to the power absorbed. The result fits the table: at two kelvins the excess is still $1.2\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ and after the third kelvin it is zero. The warming therefore continues for a long time after the concentration has stopped increasing, but it stops at a new balance.

activities.title: Conclusion: why does added carbon dioxide warm the Earth?
activities.prompt: Based on the tables, write briefly why the ground is warmer with an atmosphere and what happens when carbon dioxide is added. Use the words *balance*, *excess* and *warming*.
activities.model: With an atmosphere, the ground receives atmospheric radiation of $150\,\text{W/m}^2$ in addition to the $240\,\text{W/m}^2$ from the Sun, and in balance the surface radiates the same amount, $390\,\text{W/m}^2$. Only a warmer surface can do that, $+15\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and not $-18\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The atmosphere does not produce energy, it returns part of the radiation of the surface. When carbon dioxide is added, at first less leaves into space than is absorbed (an excess of $3.6\,\text{W/m}^2$). The excess warms the Earth, and a warming Earth radiates more, so the excess decreases. A new balance is reached when the warming is $3.6 / 1.2 = 3.0\,\text{K}$. The tables are example values of a simple model; the real values are based on satellite and surface measurements and on climate models.
criteria: I explained the warmer surface with an energy balance (in = out).
I stated that the atmosphere does not produce energy.
I described how the excess decreases as the Earth warms, and the new balance.
I distinguished the example values of the model from measurements.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the two tables and the model of energy balance. Then return to the question at the start: how can the atmosphere keep the ground warmer, even though it does not produce energy itself? Why does the frost get less harsh on a cloudy night than on a clear one?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: The area of a window is 1.5 m² and its U-value is 1.0 W/(m²·K). It is 20 °C indoors and −10 °C outdoors. A student calculates: $\Delta T = 20\,\text{K} - 10\,\text{K} = 10\,\text{K}$ and $P = UA\Delta T = 1.0\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2\text{K}} \cdot 1.5\,\text{m}^2 \cdot 10\,\text{K} = 15\,\text{W}$. Where is the error?

choices.text: The temperatures should be converted to kelvins before subtracting.
choices.feedback: A temperature difference is the same in kelvins and in degrees Celsius, so the conversion does not change the result. The error is in the sign of the outdoor temperature.

choices.text: The outdoor temperature is −10 °C, so $\Delta T = 20\,{}^\circ\text{C} - (-10\,{}^\circ\text{C}) = 30\,\text{K}$ and $P = 45\,\text{W}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. The freezing temperature is subtracted with its sign, so the difference is 30 K and not 10 K. The power is $1.0\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2\text{K}} \cdot 1.5\,\text{m}^2 \cdot 30\,\text{K} = 45\,\text{W}$, three times the student's result.

choices.text: You should divide by the U-value, because a good insulator lets less heat through.
choices.feedback: The U-value of a good insulator is small, so multiplying by it gives a small power, as it should. The U-value tells you how many watts pass through a square metre for a difference of one kelvin, so you multiply by it.

choices.text: There is no error in the calculation.
choices.feedback: Check the temperature difference. From 20 °C indoors to −10 °C outdoors is more than 10 degrees: first 20 degrees down to zero and then another 10 degrees below freezing.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: The total area of the walls, door, top and bottom of a refrigerator is 4.0 m², and their mean U-value is 0.30 W/(m²·K). It is 5 °C in the refrigerator and 21 °C in the kitchen. Heat is conducted through the walls into the refrigerator, and for the temperature of the refrigerator to stay constant, its machinery must move the same energy back to the kitchen. How much heat is conducted into the refrigerator in one day? Assume that the door is not opened. Give the answer in kilowatt-hours.
hints: In which direction does heat transfer, and what is the temperature difference between the inside and the outside?
The power conducted through the walls is $P = UA\Delta T$, and the energy in one day is $E = Pt$.

$\Delta T = 21\,{}^\circ\text{C} - 5\,{}^\circ\text{C} = 16\,\text{K}$ and $P = 0.30\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2\text{K}} \cdot 4.0\,\text{m}^2 \cdot 16\,\text{K} = 19.2\,\text{W}$. Multiply by the hours and convert to kilowatt-hours.

mistakes.feedback: You added the temperatures: $21 + 5 = 26$. Both temperatures are above zero, so the difference is $21\,{}^\circ\text{C} - 5\,{}^\circ\text{C} = 16\,\text{K}$.
This is the answer in watt-hours. A kilowatt-hour is 1000 watt-hours, so $460.8\,\text{Wh} \approx 0.46\,\text{kWh}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** $A = 4.0\,\text{m}^2$, $U = 0.30\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2\cdot\text{K}}$, $T_\text{in} = 5\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, $T_\text{kitchen} = 21\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, $t = 1\,\text{day}$; the door is not opened

**Find:** the energy $E$ conducted into the refrigerator in one day, in kilowatt-hours

**Principle:** Heat is conducted from the warm kitchen into the cold refrigerator, and when the temperatures stay constant, the power is proportional to the area and the temperature difference: $P = UA\Delta T$. The power is constant, because the door is not opened, so the energy is the power multiplied by the time.

**Formula:** $P = UA\Delta T$ and $E = Pt$, so

$$E = UA\Delta T\,t$$

**Conversions:** The temperature difference is the same in kelvins: $\Delta T = 21\,{}^\circ\text{C} - 5\,{}^\circ\text{C} = 16\,\text{K}$. The time is $t = 24\,\text{h}$, and the power is converted to kilowatts so that the energy comes out in kilowatt-hours.

**Substitution:** $P = 0.30\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2\cdot\text{K}} \cdot 4.0\,\text{m}^2 \cdot 16\,\text{K} = 19.2\,\text{W} = 0.0192\,\text{kW}$. $E = 0.0192\,\text{kW} \cdot 24\,\text{h} = 0.4608\,\text{kWh}$

**Answer:** $0.46\,\text{kWh}$, two significant figures. The limiting data are the area $4.0\,\text{m}^2$, the U-value $0.30$ and the difference of whole degrees $\Delta T = 21\,{}^\circ\text{C} - 5\,{}^\circ\text{C} = 16\,\text{K}$, all with two figures, so the calculator result $0.4608\,\text{kWh}$ is rounded.

**Reasonableness:** With rounded numbers $20\,\text{W} \cdot 24\,\text{h} \approx 0.5\,\text{kWh}$, so the result is correct. The temperature of the refrigerator stays constant only if the machinery moves the same energy out. The power is only about $20\,\text{W}$, because the temperature difference is small and the walls are well insulated. Opening the door would increase the need, because warm air would get in by convection.

activities.text: Practise further on three levels. In the Level 1 exercises one equation is enough: $P = UA\Delta T$, $E = Pt$ or energy balance. Level 3 combines heat transfer and the storage of energy.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: On a clear winter night the frost gets harsher quickly, but on a cloudy night the temperature falls only a little. What explains the difference best?

choices.text: Clouds stop the cold of space from coming to the ground.
choices.feedback: Cold is not a substance or an energy that would transfer. The ground cools because energy leaves it as thermal radiation, and the question is how much of it comes back.

choices.text: Clouds absorb the thermal radiation of the ground and radiate part of it back down, so the ground loses less energy in net terms.
choices.feedback: Correct. The water droplets and water vapour of clouds act like greenhouse gases. On a clear night a larger share of the thermal radiation of the ground escapes into space, so the surface cools faster.

choices.text: Clouds produce heat themselves.
choices.feedback: Clouds do not produce energy. They radiate down part of the energy they have absorbed from the thermal radiation of the ground, like the atmosphere in the model of the table you studied.

choices.text: Clouds stop heat from being conducted from the ground into space.
choices.feedback: Heat cannot be conducted through empty space, because there are no particles there. The Earth gives out energy into space only as thermal radiation, and clouds affect exactly that.

activities.title: 2. Energy balance of the atmosphere
activities.prompt: In the model of the first table of the Investigate stage the ground radiates 390 W/m². Of this, 100 W/m² passes straight through the atmosphere into space, and the atmosphere absorbs the rest. The atmosphere radiates 150 W/m² down to the ground. The whole Earth is in balance, so a total of 240 W/m² leaves into space. How much power per square metre does the atmosphere radiate upwards into space? The numbers are example values.
hints: What two parts does the 240 W/m² leaving into space consist of?
What leaves into space is the radiation that passed straight through from the ground and the power radiated upwards by the atmosphere: $240\,\text{W/m}^2 = 100\,\text{W/m}^2 + P_\text{up}$.
Finally check the balance of the atmosphere itself: it absorbs $390\,\text{W/m}^2 - 100\,\text{W/m}^2 = 290\,\text{W/m}^2$, and up and down together it must radiate the same amount.

mistakes.feedback: 240 W/m² is the power leaving the whole Earth into space. Of this, 100 W/m² is radiation from the ground that passes straight through the atmosphere, so the share of the atmosphere is smaller.
150 W/m² is the power radiated down by the atmosphere. The 240 W/m² leaving into space must consist of the 100 W/m² that passed straight through and the power radiated upwards by the atmosphere.

activities.solution:
**Given:** radiation of the surface $390\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$, of which $P_\text{direct} = 100\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ passes straight into space; radiated down by the atmosphere $150\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$; the total leaving into space is $P_\text{tot} = 240\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$

**Find:** the power radiated upwards into space by the atmosphere $P_\text{up}$ in $\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$

**Principle:** The whole Earth is in balance, so the power leaving into space is equal to the power absorbed from the Sun, and it consists of two parts: radiation that passes straight through from the ground and radiation sent upwards by the atmosphere. Energy is conserved, and there is no other route out.

**Formula:** The power leaving into space is the sum of the parts:

$$P_\text{direct} + P_\text{up} = P_\text{tot}$$

$$P_\text{up} = P_\text{tot} - P_\text{direct}$$

**Conversions:** No conversions are needed, because all the powers are given in the unit $\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$.

**Substitution:** $P_\text{up} = 240\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2} - 100\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2} = 140\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$

**Answer:** $140\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$, three significant figures. The example values $240$ and $100\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ are given as whole numbers, so the difference has the same precision in W/m²; no data limits it any further.

**Reasonableness:** Check the balance of the atmosphere itself: it absorbs $390 - 100 = 290\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$ and radiates $150 + 140 = 290\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$, so the atmosphere is in balance too. The result is smaller than $240\,\tfrac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2}$, because part of the power leaving into space comes straight from the surface. The atmosphere radiates slightly more down than up, because the lower air is warmer.

activities.title: 3. Explain and transfer
activities.prompt: Your friend claims: "The Earth radiates as much energy into space as it absorbs from the Sun, so extra carbon dioxide cannot change its temperature. Besides, the greenhouse effect is entirely harmful." Use energy balance and thermal radiation to explain what is right and what is wrong in the claim.
criteria: I say that in balance the power coming in and the power going out are equal and the temperature stays constant.
I explain that extra carbon dioxide absorbs more of the thermal radiation of the ground, so for a while less leaves into space than is absorbed.
I explain that the Earth warms until it again radiates as much as it absorbs, that is, a new balance settles at a higher temperature.
I state that the natural greenhouse effect keeps the ground at about +15 °C instead of about −18 °C, and the problem is its strengthening.
activities.model: The first part of the claim is true in a state of balance: when the Earth radiates into space the same power as it absorbs from the Sun, its temperature stays constant. The balance is not permanent, however. When carbon dioxide is added, the atmosphere absorbs more of the thermal radiation of the ground and radiates part of it back down, and for a while less power leaves into space than the Earth absorbs. The extra power warms the oceans, the land and the air. A warmer Earth radiates more, so the warming continues until the power leaving is again equal to the power absorbed. A new balance therefore settles at a higher temperature. The greenhouse effect is not entirely harmful either: the natural greenhouse effect raises the mean temperature of the ground from about −18 °C to about +15 °C. The problem is its strengthening because of human emissions.

activities.text: Finally, three quick questions. Answer first yourself and open the answer only afterwards.
